question: Is everything fixed by destiny (niyati), or do effort and deeds shape a being's course?

sides.position: (As reported by opponents) Everything is fixed: there is no cause for defilement or purification, no exertion, strength, energy or human effort; beings are transformed by destiny, circumstance and nature and reach the end of suffering after a fixed round that no vow or austerity can shorten.
arguments: the ball of string runs out of itself (DN 2)
we do not pass beyond destiny, as the ocean does not pass its shore (Ja 545)
suffering is neither self-made nor other-made but saṅgatiya (Sūtr 1.1.2)

sides.position: Deeds, action and energy are effective; all Buddhas teach it; there is an element of initiative, and beings are seen to initiate. Destiny, God's creation and no-cause alike end in inaction.
arguments: Makkhali's doctrine is the worst, like a hair blanket (AN 3.137)
one who comes and goes of himself cannot deny self-doing (AN 6.38)
the doctrine of cause is the safe wager (MN 60)
only one Ājīvaka reached heaven in 91 aeons, and he taught deeds (MN 71)

sides.position: Effort exists: the Ājīvika potter makes his pots by effort and would punish one who broke them; a god gained his state by exertion. In the developed doctrine niyati is one of five co-causes, wrong only when taken alone.
arguments: the five causes together are right view (Sanmati 3.53)

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Ājīvika position as reported denies effort any role, and the Buddhist position rejects destiny as a cause; no principle joins them without erasing one side.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Jain synthesis (Sanmati 3.53) treats niyati and effort as co-causes seen from different standpoints — the tradition's own reconciliation, but it rejects exactly the Ājīvika claim that effort is nothing.
P1-level: fixity might describe the whole round seen at once, effort the being's lived course — no text proposes this for the Ājīvikas.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Ājīvikas (as reported): 'there is no exertion'. Buddhists: destiny is one of the tenets that end in inaction (AN 3.61). Jains accept the five-cause synthesis but call one-sided niyati false view.

historical_debates.name: Mahāvīra and Saddālaputta
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Jain: the Ājīvika potter is converted

question: Do good and bad deeds bear fruit (kiriyavāda) or not (akiriyavāda)?

sides.position: (As reported) Pūraṇa: the doer of any violence does no evil, the giver gains no merit; Pakudha: the seven bodies are unmade and unaffected, so no one kills; Ajita: there is no fruit of good and bad deeds.
arguments: a heap of flesh made of all beings brings no evil (DN 2)
the sword passes between the seven bodies (DN 2)

sides.position: (As reported) There is no unseen potency of deeds; things differ by own-nature; merit and demerit are not; the rites bear no fruit.
arguments: fire is hot and water cold by svabhāva
no one returns from the other world

sides.position: Deeds bear fruit; the doctrine of action is the safe course; Gosāla's 'no deed' is the worst doctrine.
arguments: the six classes are by conduct (AN 6.57)

sides.position: The true kiriyavāda knows influx, bondage and the wearing away of karma; the akiriyavādins, who call the world barren and fixed, are like a blind man with a lamp.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the deniers explicitly reject any fruit of deeds; the affirmers make it the ground of the holy life.
candidate_readings: P1-level: 'no doer, no killer' (Pakudha) might be read as a statement about unchanging substance (ultimate) against the conventional reality of harm — the Buddhist and Jain reporters reject this as licence for killing.
P5-neyartha: none — no source treats the akiriya teaching as provisional.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Buddhist and Jain reporters call the akiriya teachings a negation of the holy life (MN 76); the reported Pūraṇa would reject any reconciliation that restores merit and demerit.

question: Does anything survive the body's death — is there another world and rebirth, or is consciousness a product of the body that ends with it?

sides.position: (As reported) Consciousness arises from the four elements formed into a body, like intoxicating power, and perishes with them; there is no one who goes to another world, so there is none; the burnt body does not return; no one comes back to tell.
arguments: 'I am fat' shows the body is the self

sides.position: (As reported) Ajita: the person of four elements is annihilated at death; there is no other world.
arguments: the elements return to their masses (DN 2)

sides.position: There is another world; the denier loses the wager either way; Kumāra Kassapa answers each of Pāyāsi's arguments with a simile; Śāntarakṣita argues that a first cognition presupposes a prior one, so mind is a beginningless continuum.
arguments: dream, hot iron ball, conch, fire-sticks (DN 23)

sides.position: The soul is other than the body: Kesi answers Paesi; the Sūtrakṛtāṅga answers the five-element and soul-is-body teachers.
arguments: they go from darkness to darkness

sides.position: The self is distinct from the body: consciousness is absent in the corpse, and what experiences the elements cannot be one of them.
Having granted a knower that lasts through the body, the suśikṣita Cārvāka cannot show a cause of its destruction; so it is eternal and passes to other bodies.
arguments: no cause of destruction of a partless self

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Lokāyata explicitly denies another world and a surviving self; every other party affirms them.
candidate_readings: P1-level: the Lokāyata speaks only of what perception establishes (the vyāvahārika world) — but it denies, not merely brackets, the other world.
P2-standpoint: the suśikṣita Cārvāka's 'a knower lasting as long as the body' concedes part of the opponents' case (Jayanta) — a partial convergence on the living knower only.
P6-upaya: the tradition's account that Bṛhaspati taught the doctrine to delude the asuras (Maitrī Up. 7.9) makes it a deliberate device — a reading the Cārvākas as reported would reject.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Cārvāka (as reported) calls talk of the other world a priests' livelihood; all opponents call the Cārvāka view the root of wrong conduct.

notes: Related existing disputes: dsp:consciousness-from-elements (U09), dsp:validity-of-inference (U11), dsp:jabali-rama (U05).

question: Is the soul the same as the body, or different from it?

sides.position: (As reported) The same: the soul is bounded by the skin; no soul can be drawn out and shown like a sword from its sheath; when the body is burnt nothing arises again.
Different: the soul is other than the body (Kesi to Paesi).
Neither view is taught: 'soul is body' and 'soul is other than body' both make the holy life impossible; the Tathāgata teaches by the middle, dependent origination.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the materialist and the Jain affirm opposite answers; the Buddhist declines both.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Buddhist 'middle' is itself offered as avoiding two standpoints — but it does not accept either side's claim.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each party insists on its own answer; the Buddhist texts count both others as extremes.

question: Should one refuse to affirm or deny anything about what lies beyond experience (the other world, fruit of deeds, the perfected one after death)?

sides.position: (As reported) Yes: to every such question, in each of its four forms, 'I do not say it is so, nor thus, nor otherwise, nor not so, nor not not so'; knowing is useless and ignorance better.
arguments: avoids false speech, grasping, and refutation (DN 1)
who knows whether the soul exists, and what use is knowing it? (Śīlāṅka)

sides.position: It is eel-wriggling born of fear or dullness; yet the Buddha himself sets some questions aside as not leading to the goal and declares what he knows beyond all views.
arguments: MN 76: the dull teacher is an unreliable holy life
DN 16: the Buddha sets aside Subhadda's question about the six

sides.position: The ignorant cannot settle their inquiry in ignorance or teach others; they are blind leading the blind.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Ajñānika refuses to assert; Buddhist and Jain both assert, and both insist their own reticence (the undeclared points; the 'inexpressible' of the sevenfold predication) differs in kind from his.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Sañjaya's refusal of four alternatives resembles the Jain 'avaktavya' and the later catuṣkoṭi — a resemblance noted by scholars (metadata only), rejected by both traditions.
P4-stage: the Buddha's setting-aside is tied to what benefits the hearer — not a general refusal.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Jains: syādvāda asserts under a standpoint, ajñāna asserts nothing. Buddhists: the Buddha knows and declares what is beyond views; the eel-wriggler knows nothing.

question: Was Gosāla Mahāvīra's disciple and a false Jina, or an independent Jina in his seventh reanimation?

sides.position: Gosāla was Maṅkhali's son and Mahāvīra's disciple for six years; he falsely claimed to be a Jina, burnt two monks, was undone by his own fiery power, and confessed on his deathbed.

(Ājīvika claim, known only from the Jain report) The disciple Gosāla is dead; the one speaking is Udāyi Kuṇḍiyāyaṇa in his seventh reanimation, a Jina and the last tīrthaṅkara of the age; Mahāvīra has changed from a solitary ascetic to a teacher of crowds.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a question of fact and legitimacy recorded only by one party; no principle applies.
candidate_readings: None proposed; the Ājīvika side has no surviving voice.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Jain account itself ends with Gosāla's confession; the Ājīvika claim survives only inside it.

historical_debates.name: The confrontation at Sāvatthī
historical_debates.date: (Jain account) sixteen years before Mahāvīra's death
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Jain: Gosāla's fire returns on him; he dies in seven days and repents

question: How many means of knowledge are valid?

sides.position: (As reported) Perception alone — inference fails because pervasion cannot be known.
arguments: no means establishes vyāpti; upādhi cannot be excluded

sides.position: (Purandara) Inference as known in the world is valid; only inference to the transcendent is rejected.
arguments: worldly inference vs inference beyond the worldly path

sides.position: (Suśikṣita Cārvākas; Jayarāśi) The number cannot be fixed; no definition of any means of knowledge can be made good.
arguments: circularity of every definition of perception and inference

sides.position: Perception and inference; one who denies inference uses it to convey his intention, and the world itself infers causes from effects.

notes: U33 contribution (Lokāyata sides). U50 owns this dispute and its reconciliation; none is proposed here.

question: The status of the Veda: authorless, God-authored, or rejected?

sides.position: (As reported) Rejected: the Veda is tainted by falsehood, inconsistency and repetition; its makers were buffoons, knaves and demons; its rites are a livelihood of priests; the Bārhaspatyas call it a mere cover.
arguments: the slain beast and the sacrificer's father

sides.position: (As reported) Ajita: there is no gift, no sacrifice, no offering.
Sacrifice of animals and claims of birth-purity are refuted; the priests are cheats (Bhūridatta).
arguments: if the slain go to heaven, let brāhmaṇas slay brāhmaṇas

sides.position: The charge of falsehood, inconsistency (vyāghāta) and repetition fails: a failed rite is due to defects in the act, agent or means.

notes: U33 contribution; U50 owns the dispute and its reconciliation.

question: Is there a self?

sides.position: (As reported) Only the living body qualified by consciousness; nothing survives it.
(As reported) Pakudha: the soul is one of seven eternal, unmoving bodies.
(As reported) Not declared: 'who knows whether the soul exists?'
A self distinct from the body exists: consciousness is absent in the corpse.

notes: U33 contribution (śramaṇa and Lokāyata sides); U50 owns the dispute.

question: Is Īśvara real, needed, or a special puruṣa?

sides.position: (As reported) The only lord is the king known to the world; variety comes from own-nature.
Those who say the world was made by gods, Brahmā, Īśvara, pradhāna or the self-born do not know the truth; the world never perishes.
If Brahmā were lord of the world, why did he make it unhappy and unjust? Creation by God is a tenet that ends in inaction.

notes: U33 contribution; U50 owns the dispute.
